title: From Moineau's to the Hamlet: Potlatch, Two Counterfeit Novels, and the Long Afterward
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Paris, the sixteenth arrondissement: birth
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (Yale Beinecke finding aid, GEN MSS 1556, which reads only 'Michèle Bernstein (1932- ) is a French writer'). The day, 28 April 1932, rests on fr. and en.wikipedia alone; no primary document giving it was reached. The arrondissement comes from a fr.wikipedia category and is the weakest element here. The coordinate is the 16e rather than the generic Paris pin the research pool used, which sat on the Île de la Cité, 5.5 km east.
stops.campa: A daughter is born in the sixteenth arrondissement to Russian Jewish parents. Her father, Michel Bernstein, deals in old books, and within ten years that trade in paper will have another use and the family name will appear in the records of a clandestine printing operation. The archive that will one day hold her letters records only the year of this day. Two encyclopaedias supply the twenty-eighth of April. No birth certificate has surfaced in any of them.
suggested_refs: The Michèle Bernstein Papers, GEN MSS 1556, Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University
sources: Yale Beinecke, Guide to the Michèle Bernstein Papers (GEN MSS 1556)

stops.name: Paris, rue de Lourmel: the false papers
stops.date_confidence: 1942 attested for the Défense de la France network's mass production of false papers and for Michel Bernstein's involvement (fr.wikipedia, 'Défense de la France', naming 'l'implication du libraire Michel Bernstein'; fr.wikipedia, '15e arrondissement de Paris', siting the workshops with printers and booksellers of the quarter on the rue de Lourmel). Month and day unrecorded, defaulted to 01-01. The February start, the collaborator Monique Rollin, and the forging manual reported in the dossier were confirmed nowhere and are not stated. Michèle Bernstein's own whereabouts under the occupation are undocumented in every source reached: the household is attested, the child is not.
stops.campa: In the fifteenth arrondissement, among the printers and booksellers of the rue de Lourmel, the network called Défense de la France runs off false identity cards by the tens of thousands. The papers have to be good enough to keep the bearer alive. Michel Bernstein, bookseller, is named in the accounts of that work. His daughter is ten years old and Jewish in an occupied city. Where she spends these years is written down nowhere at all: not in the network's records, not in the family's, not in anything the archives have collected since.
suggested_refs: The false-papers workshops of the Défense de la France network, rue de Lourmel, Paris 15e
sources: Musée de la Résistance en ligne, biography of Michel Bernstein (dossier-relayed, not re-fetched)

stops.name: Paris, the Sorbonne: a year of boredom
stops.date_confidence: 1952 attested (fr.wikipedia: 'En 1952, elle étudie à la Sorbonne mais s'y ennuie'); the Yale finding aid gives the studies without a year. Month and day unrecorded, defaulted to 01-01. Coordinate corrected to the building at 1 rue Victor Cousin; the research pool's pin sat 230 m south.
stops.campa: She enrols at the Sorbonne in 1952. The lecture halls of the fifth arrondissement stand half a kilometre from the bars where the Lettrists drink, and the distance decides the matter. Nothing survives to say what she read, how long she stayed, or whether she took a degree; the archive that will hold her correspondence for seventy years holds not one page of coursework. The single sentence that fixes the year fixes the mood along with it: en 1952, elle étudie à la Sorbonne mais s'y ennuie.
suggested_refs: The Sorbonne, 1 rue Victor Cousin, Paris 5e
sources: Yale Beinecke, Guide to the Michèle Bernstein Papers

stops.name: Paris, rue du Four: Chez Moineau
stops.date_confidence: 1952 attested for her entry into the Moineau circle (fr.wikipedia: 'Chez Moineau, un bistrot situé 22, rue du Four') and for her meeting with Debord (Yale finding aid). No month is recorded; February is an ordering device only. The coordinate is the pin guy_debord.journey.json already carries for its rue du Four stop, inherited unchanged; the research pool had put the bar on the rue de la Huchette, 900 m east, which is the wrong street.
stops.campa: At 22 rue du Four there is a bar where the drinkers are eighteen, twenty, twenty-two, and nobody works. Bernstein arrives from the Sorbonne, where she is bored, and stays. She is closest here to Jean-Claude Guilbert and to Patrick Straram, not yet to Guy Debord, who is drinking at the same tables and whom she meets this year. Nobody in the room has published anything. Photographs get taken all the same, and seventy years later they sit boxed in a Yale reading room, catalogued by name, filed as Series I.
suggested_refs: Chez Moineau, 22 rue du Four, Paris 6e
The Moineau photographs in the Michèle Bernstein Papers, Yale
sources: Yale Beinecke, Guide to the Michèle Bernstein Papers, Series I

stops.name: Le Havre, the settings of the novel
stops.date_confidence: August 1952 attested (fr.wikipedia, which names Guilbert and Straram and gives the purpose of the trip). Day unrecorded, defaulted to 01. Coordinate is the centre of Le Havre; no address is given in the source.
stops.campa: In August she goes to Le Havre with Guilbert and Straram to look at the settings of a novel. Jean-Paul Sartre had put Antoine Roquentin in a port city he called Bouville, built out of this one, and the three of them go to stand in it. They are visiting a book laid over streets that know nothing about it. It is the only journey out of Paris recorded for her in these years, and what they did once they arrived, whether they found the places Sartre used or only walked the docks, no source says.
suggested_refs: Jean-Paul Sartre, La Nausée (1938), whose Bouville is built from Le Havre

stops.name: Paris, 15 rue Duguay-Trouin: Potlatch 3
stops.date_confidence: 6 July 1954 attested on the issue itself (facsimile and transcription at oeuvresouvertes.wordpress.com), which also carries the masthead address. Coordinate corrected to 15 rue Duguay-Trouin; the research pool's pin was 330 m off. The claim that the byline Ivich is borrowed from Sartre's Les Chemins de la liberté is a bare dossier assertion, unsupported in anything reached, and is not made here.
stops.campa: Potlatch number three is dated the sixth of July. It costs nothing, is not sold anywhere, and goes out by post to people the group finds interesting. Inside is a short piece signed Michèle-Ivich Bernstein, setting the Lettrist International beside the Jacobins and the Cordeliers, and a declaration on Guatemala carrying her name among the signatures. The masthead gives an address, 15 rue Duguay-Trouin in the sixth, which is not an office of any kind but André-Frank Conord's flat.
suggested_refs: Potlatch no. 3, 6 July 1954, bulletin of the Lettrist International
sources: oeuvresouvertes.wordpress.com, facsimile and transcription of Potlatch no. 3

stops.name: Paris: the marriage to Guy Debord
stops.date_confidence: 17 August 1954 attested (fr.wikipedia, which names both witnesses; en.wikipedia gives the same date). The Yale finding aid gives the year only and does not carry the date, contrary to the research pool's citation. No source names the mairie, and the coordinate is the Paris pin guy_debord.journey.json carries for this marriage, inherited unchanged.
stops.campa: They marry on the seventeenth of August. Mohamed Dahou stands witness for Debord and André-Frank Conord for Bernstein; twelve days later Conord is excluded from the Lettrist International, which is how that organisation conducts its friendships. She is twenty-two, and so is he. No source names the town hall. No photograph of the day has surfaced, and no account written since says who else was in the room. The marriage will last until January 1972.
suggested_refs: The exclusion of André-Frank Conord from the Lettrist International, 29 August 1954

stops.name: Paris, square des Missions-Étrangères: Potlatch 16
stops.date_confidence: Issue and date attested (notbored.org/bernstein.html, which lists the title under 26 January 1955). The text itself was not read in any pass, so nothing is said here about its content. Coordinate is the square off the rue du Bac.
stops.campa: Potlatch sixteen, dated the twenty-sixth of January, carries a piece of hers titled with the name of a small square off the rue du Bac, in the seventh arrondissement. The square is a garden behind a wall. A Left Bank place name has been lifted into a bulletin otherwise concerned with revolution and the demolition of cities. Why, or what happened there, the surviving record does not say. An index entry gives the title and the date. The text itself has not been recovered.
suggested_refs: Potlatch no. 16, 26 January 1955
The square des Missions-Étrangères, rue du Bac, Paris 7e

stops.name: Cosio d'Arroscia: the founding
stops.date_confidence: 28 July 1957 attested (fr.wikipedia; en.wikipedia's article on Bernstein gives the same day). guy_debord.journey.json dates the founding 27-28 July and en.wikipedia's article on the Situationist International gives only 'July 1957'; the disagreement is recorded here and not resolved. Coordinate inherited byte-identically from guy_debord.journey.json.
stops.campa: A handful of people meet in a village in the Ligurian hills and sign the founding of the Situationist International. Bernstein and Debord come as the Lettrist International; Asger Jorn, Giuseppe Pinot-Gallizio and Piero Simondo come from the Imaginist Bauhaus; Ralph Rumney arrives as the entire membership of the London Psychogeographical Association. Sixteen years later Rumney will be her second husband. The sources disagree over whether the meeting ran one day or two, and over the date inside July. She is twenty-five.
suggested_refs: The founding conference of the Situationist International, Cosio d'Arroscia, July 1957
sources: Yale Beinecke, Guide to the Michèle Bernstein Papers

stops.name: Paris: the lumpensecretariat
stops.date_confidence: 1957 attested from her own 2013 preface (theanarchistlibrary.org), which gives the year, the publishing house, and the journal's circulation. Month unrecorded; September is an ordering device. The research pool's paraphrase, that she called the period 'her lumpen secretariat', reverses her wording: she writes that she was a member of the lumpensecretariat. Coordinate is a general Paris pin, no address being recorded.
stops.campa: The organisation founded in Liguria has a journal, and the journal sells five or six copies an issue; the rest are posted to people the group finds interesting. Debord is not working. Bernstein has a job at a publishing house she will call humdrum, for wages she will count in English pennies, and the household runs on it. She also writes copy for a horse-racing newspaper. Debord tells Henri Lefebvre she casts horoscopes for the horses, and Lefebvre repeats it as fact.
stops.quote: In those days I was still a member of the lumpensecretariat, working for tuppence ha'penny at a humdrum publishing house.
stops.quote_source: Michèle Bernstein, 'Preface in the Guise of an Autobiography, or Vice Versa' (2013)
suggested_refs: Internationale Situationniste, the journal's early print runs and distribution
sources: Michèle Bernstein, 'Preface in the Guise of an Autobiography, or Vice Versa' (2013), theanarchistlibrary.org

stops.name: Paris: the fake popular novel
stops.date_confidence: 1957-58 attested from the 2013 preface, which gives both the motive and the year. Month is an ordering device; the dossier's 'end of 1957, continuing into 1958' is a precision the preface does not support and is not carried here. Coordinate is a general Paris pin.
stops.campa: Being skint has an obvious remedy for someone who can write, and she takes it. The plan is a counterfeit: a light novel of the kind that sells, aimed at the market Françoise Sagan has just proved exists, written to be sold rather than to be meant. The book that comes out of the plan détourns Les Liaisons dangereuses and moves the libertines to Saint-Germain-des-Prés. She works at it through 1957 and 1958. Her own account of the motive, set down fifty-six years later, is one sentence long.
stops.quote: The solution was simple: I would fabricate a 'fake' popular novel.
stops.quote_source: Michèle Bernstein, 'Preface in the Guise of an Autobiography, or Vice Versa' (2013)
suggested_refs: Choderlos de Laclos, Les Liaisons dangereuses, the model détourned in Tous les chevaux du roi
sources: Michèle Bernstein, 'Preface in the Guise of an Autobiography, or Vice Versa' (2013), theanarchistlibrary.org

stops.name: Paris: no useless leniency
stops.date_confidence: Attested to Internationale Situationniste no. 1, Paris, June 1958 (bopsecrets.org, Ken Knabb translation, carrying the issue's own source note; that page is headed 'excerpts'). Day unrecorded, defaulted to 01. Coordinate is a general Paris pin: no editorial address appears in the source.
stops.campa: The first issue of Internationale Situationniste appears in June, and her essay in it is about who may be admired. Indiscriminate praise, she argues, is a form of cowardice; a group that experiments on its own daily life cannot keep its judgements apart from its friendships and should not pretend to. In her own text the words intellectual and artistic carry scare quotes. Most of the journal is unsigned, on the principle that ideas belong to the organisation. This piece is signed.
stops.quote: "Intellectual" or "artistic" collaboration in a group devoted to the type of experimentation we are engaged in involves our everyday life. It is always accompanied with an element of friendship.
stops.quote_source: Michèle Bernstein, 'Pas d'indulgences inutiles', Internationale Situationniste no. 1, June 1958, trans. Ken Knabb
suggested_refs: Internationale Situationniste no. 1, Paris, June 1958

stops.name: Paris, rue Descartes: La Méthode
stops.date_confidence: October 1958 attested (fr.wikipedia, naming the founder Jacques Florencie and the site facing the École polytechnique; the Beinecke collection page has her as the manager for several months in 1958). Day unrecorded, defaulted to 01. The house number 2, the opening poster of 10 October, and the advertised drink prices reported in the dossier were confirmed nowhere; the coordinate is the street, not a building, and is corrected from the research pool's pin 180 m southwest.
stops.campa: A cabaret opens on the rue Descartes, facing the École polytechnique, founded by a singer and guitarist named Jacques Florencie with Debord's backing. Bernstein takes it on as artistic manager and keeps the post for several months of that autumn and winter. It is the only business she is ever recorded as running. No house number survives, and no accounts, and nobody wrote down when it closed. A library catalogue lists a folder of documents about the place and calls her the manager. Nothing else has been located.
suggested_refs: La Méthode, cabaret, rue Descartes, Paris 5e, 1958

segments.name: Two Novels and a Television Studio

stops.name: Paris, Saint-Germain-des-Prés: Tous les chevaux du roi
stops.date_confidence: 1960 attested for the year (Yale finding aid) and for the publisher (fr.wikipedia, which also notes that Buchet-Chastel later published Debord's own book); the research pool cited Yale for the publisher, which Yale does not name. Month and day unrecorded, defaulted to 01-01. Coordinate marks the Saint-Germain-des-Prés publishing district; the firm's 1960 street address was not confirmed.
stops.campa: Buchet/Chastel publishes Tous les chevaux du roi. Seven years later the same house will publish La Société du spectacle, by her husband, and the two books will sit in one catalogue. The novel is taken for a Sagan imitation, which is exactly what it was built to be, and it sells. Its narrator is a woman who watches her husband's affairs with an equanimity readers find shocking or modern depending on the decade they read it in. In September she goes on television to talk about it.
suggested_refs: Michèle Bernstein, Tous les chevaux du roi (Buchet/Chastel, 1960)
John Kelsey's translation, All the King's Horses (Semiotext(e), 2008), with an afterword by Odile Passot
sources: Yale Beinecke, Guide to the Michèle Bernstein Papers
editions-allia.com, Tous les chevaux du roi

stops.name: Paris: the Pinot-Gallizio monograph with Asger Jorn
stops.date_confidence: 1960 attested from the Yale finding aid, Series II, which dates the proof and names both authors. Month is an ordering device. Le long voyage, which the dossier proposed as possibly hers, is listed in the same finding aid under Jorn and Pierre Wemaëre and is not attributed to her here. Coordinate is a general Paris pin; the imprint's address is not given.
stops.campa: With Asger Jorn she writes the monograph on Giuseppe Pinot-Gallizio, the pharmacist from Alba who paints industrial painting by the metre and sells it the same way. It goes into the Bibliothèque d'Alexandrie, an imprint run out of Jorn's Scandinavian Institute for Comparative Vandalism. The proof copy that survives is dated 1960 and carries both their names. Photographs from these years show her with Jorn and with Debord, indoors, a glass in her hand.
suggested_refs: Michèle Bernstein and Asger Jorn, Pinot-Gallizio, Bibliothèque d'Alexandrie (1960)
sources: Yale Beinecke, Guide to the Michèle Bernstein Papers, Series II

stops.name: Paris, rue Cognacq-Jay: Lectures pour tous
stops.date_confidence: 14 September 1960 attested, with a running time of 8 min 08 s, from the INA catalogue record; the research pool cited editions-allia.com, which says nothing of the broadcast. Pierre Dumayet as interviewer is dossier-supplied and unconfirmed. The coordinate is the RTF studios at rue Cognacq-Jay and is a hedge: the pool's pin was the Maison de la Radio, which did not open until December 1963 and cannot have carried a 1960 television broadcast.
stops.campa: The broadcast runs eight minutes and eight seconds and goes out in September, on a programme called Lectures pour tous. She is twenty-eight and answers questions about a book whose whole procedure is that it is not sincere, on a programme built on the assumption that authors are. The recording survives in the national audiovisual catalogue. Neither the studio nor the interviewer is named in that record, though every account of the broadcast gives Pierre Dumayet.
suggested_refs: INA, 'Michèle Bernstein: Tous les chevaux du roi', Lectures pour tous, 14 September 1960
sources: INA catalogue record, Lectures pour tous, 14 September 1960

stops.name: Paris, Saint-Germain-des-Prés: La Nuit
stops.date_confidence: 1961 attested for the year (Yale finding aid) and for the publisher (fr.wikipedia). The nouveau-roman framing comes from Éditions Allia's own page for the book and from fr.wikipedia's description of it as a pastiche; the Yale finding aid says nothing of Robbe-Grillet, contrary to the research pool's citation. Month and day unrecorded, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: The second novel tells the plot of the first one over again, coldly, in the manner arriving around her as she writes it: Robbe-Grillet, Sarraute, Simon, Duras, Butor. Same three people, same triangle, no warmth anywhere in it. Buchet/Chastel publishes it in 1961, the same house as the first, and it sells less than the counterfeit that came before. Éditions Allia will reprint it fifty-two years on, and an English edition will appear the same year under the title The Night. She is twenty-nine, and this is the last novel she publishes.
suggested_refs: Michèle Bernstein, La Nuit (Buchet/Chastel, 1961; Éditions Allia, 2013)
Clodagh Kinsella's translation, The Night (Book Works, 2013)
sources: Yale Beinecke, Guide to the Michèle Bernstein Papers

stops.name: Paris, rue Monge: the fifth and the sixth on foot
stops.date_confidence: Not a dated event. The stop marks the geography of the two novels as Bernstein herself describes it in her 2013 preface, which names the fifth and sixth arrondissements and singles out the rue Monge. The date orders the stop after the second novel and records no occurrence. Coordinate is the rue Monge.
stops.campa: Her characters cross almost every street of the fifth and the sixth arrondissements, and the rue Monge by name. The geography is invented in the sense that the people are, and not invented at all: she walked these streets in order to write them, on drifts with no destination, letting the buildings decide the turning. A reader who wanted to could walk the book. Fifty years later she sets down in a preface what the practice was, and refuses the word hobby for it.
stops.quote: The dérive wasn't a hobby, we wanted to make it a way of life. Letting our steps guide us through the city (the dérive is urban) without following a set path or pursuing any particular goal.
stops.quote_source: Michèle Bernstein, 'Preface in the Guise of an Autobiography, or Vice Versa' (2013)
suggested_refs: The rue Monge and the dérive geography of La Nuit
sources: Michèle Bernstein, 'Preface in the Guise of an Autobiography, or Vice Versa' (2013), theanarchistlibrary.org

stops.name: Paris: Sunset Boulevard in the seventh issue
stops.date_confidence: April 1962, issue 7, attested (notbored.org/bernstein.html, which lists the piece). Day unrecorded, defaulted to 01. Coordinate is a general Paris pin; no editorial address is given in the source.
stops.campa: Issue seven of the journal, April 1962, carries a piece of hers called Sunset Boulevard. The title is Billy Wilder's, taken and turned somewhere it was never meant to go, which is what the group means by détournement. Most of the journal remains unsigned, on the principle that ideas belong to the organisation and not to whoever happened to write the sentence. Her name is on this one. Copies go out by post to people the organisation finds interesting, as they have since Potlatch.
suggested_refs: Internationale situationniste no. 7, April 1962

stops.name: Antwerp: the month of the sixth conference
stops.date_confidence: The photograph is attested to Antwerp, November 1962 (notbored.org/bernstein.html), which gives no occasion for the trip. The sixth conference of the Situationist International, 12-16 November 1962, is attested (fr.wikipedia) and is carried in guy_debord.journey.json at this coordinate, inherited byte-identically. Her attendance is a reconstruction from the coincidence of month and city, is asserted by no source, and is not asserted in the campa.
stops.campa: A photograph dated November 1962 puts her in Antwerp. That same month the Situationist International holds its sixth conference in the city, from the twelfth to the sixteenth, in a room that would comfortably hold every member. The break with the artists has already happened, and what is left of the organisation publishes a journal and expels people. Whether she was at the conference or in Antwerp for some other reason the photograph does not say, and no minutes name her.
suggested_refs: Proceedings of the sixth conference of the Situationist International, Antwerp, 12-16 November 1962

stops.name: Odense: Destruction of RSG-6
stops.date_confidence: June 1963 and the exhibition's contents are attested from Debord's own catalogue text for the show (bopsecrets.org/SI/newforms.htm), which places it in Denmark under J. V. Martin and names Bernstein's Victories. The city Odense and the venue Galerie EXI come from the dossier and a journal abstract and could not be re-confirmed: both pages that would have done so returned HTTP 404. Coordinate corrected to Odense, the research pool's pin sitting 1.2 km east. Day unrecorded, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: In Denmark the group mounts a show against the British civil defence plan for nuclear war. J. V. Martin hangs his thermonuclear maps, Debord shows painted directives, and a bomb shelter is built inside the gallery. Bernstein's contribution is a set of small reliefs made from painted toy soldiers, each titled as a victory: the Paris Commune, the Spanish Republicans, the Grande Jacquerie. Every one of those was a defeat. The originals are reported lost.
suggested_refs: Michèle Bernstein, Victoires du prolétariat (1963), reliefs shown at Destruction of RSG-6
Guy Debord, 'The Situationists and the New Forms of Action in Politics or Art', catalogue text for the exhibition

stops.name: Paris: the proofs corrected in two hands
stops.date_confidence: The proofs are dated 1958 to 1964 in the Yale finding aid, Series II, which records manuscript corrections in both Debord's hand and Bernstein's; the Contre le cinéma material is dated 1964. The stop's date orders the sequence and marks no single occurrence. Coordinate is a general Paris pin: no working address is recorded anywhere.
stops.campa: The boxes that will go to Yale hold the maquettes and proofs of the journal, issues one through nine, and most of them are corrected in two hands, his and hers. There are also her typographical corrections on the proofs of Debord's Contre le cinéma, filed in the same series as the screenplays of two of his films. The finding aid dates the material 1958 to 1964, which is the whole life of the journal to that point. It does not say which hand made which mark, only that both are present on the same sheets.
suggested_refs: Proofs and maquettes of Internationale Situationniste nos. 1-9, Michèle Bernstein Papers, Yale
Guy Debord, Contre le cinéma (1964), proofs with her corrections
sources: Yale Beinecke, Guide to the Michèle Bernstein Papers, Series II

stops.name: Paris: the note for the Times Literary Supplement
stops.date_confidence: 3 September 1964 attested from the Yale finding aid, which matches the surviving proof to the Times Literary Supplement text of that date. Composition took place in Paris and publication in London; the stop sits where she was. Coordinate is a general Paris pin.
stops.campa: She writes a short account of the organisation for an English readership, and the Times Literary Supplement prints it on the third of September. It explains the expulsions, by now the group's most famous habit, as nothing more than the practice of taking one's own declarations at their word. It is written in Paris and printed in London, and she does not travel for it. A proof survives at Yale, matching the printed text of that date. The finding aid gives her name for it in brackets.
stops.quote: The situationists immediately exclude from their ranks those who cease to support any of the group's rigorous positions in practice, for which they have often been reproached: it seems an excessive manner of taking their own declarations seriously.
stops.quote_source: Michèle Bernstein, 'Note on the Situationist International' (1964), NOT BORED! translation
suggested_refs: Michèle Bernstein, 'Note on the Situationist International', Times Literary Supplement, 3 September 1964
sources: Yale Beinecke, Guide to the Michèle Bernstein Papers, Series II
notbored.org, 'Note on the Situationist International' PDF

stops.name: Paris: the Lewinian epic
stops.date_confidence: 1964 attested from the Yale finding aid, Series I, which describes the 22 autograph poems, the grouping of seventeen as Épopée Léwinienne, the circumstances of the breakup, and the accompanying notebook in Bernstein's hand. Month unrecorded; November is an ordering device. Coordinate is a general Paris pin.
stops.campa: Twenty-two poems in Debord's hand arrive, seventeen of them gathered under a title built from the name of the man she has left him for: Walter Lewino, a journalist. She keeps them. She also writes a notebook explaining them and files it with the poems, so that whoever eventually opens the box will understand what the jokes are about. The notebook is still with the poems fifty-five years later, listed on the same line of a library's finding aid, in her hand.
suggested_refs: Guy Debord, Épopée Léwinienne and five further poems, 1964, with Bernstein's explanatory notebook, Yale
sources: Yale Beinecke, Guide to the Michèle Bernstein Papers, Series I

stops.name: Aarhus: Ny-irrealisme
stops.date_confidence: March 1967 attested from the Situationist International chronology for 1967 (cddc.vt.edu), which names the operation and the work shown. Day unrecorded; 15 is an ordering device inside the month. Coordinate is Aarhus. This episode appears in no part of the original dossier and was found in the interlock pass.
stops.campa: At an operation called Ny-irrealisme in Aarhus she shows the Victory of the Spanish Republicans again, four years after the Danish room with the bomb shelter in it. It is the second time the Danish section has hung her painted soldiers on a wall, and the last time she exhibits with the group anywhere. The Spanish Republicans lost their war in 1939 and the relief insists they won it. Three months after this she resigns. The day within March is not recorded, no photograph of the hang has been found, and the chronology that carries the exhibition gives it a single line.
suggested_refs: The Ny-irrealisme operation, Aarhus, March 1967

stops.name: Paris: the resignation over a war
stops.date_confidence: June 1967 attested from the Situationist International chronology (cddc.vt.edu), which also records that she went on exhibiting and associating informally for about three years afterward. Her stated reason and the quoted line come from the Frieze interview 'The Game' (2013), reached only through a text proxy after frieze.com returned HTTP 403. The rival account, that she was expelled for Zionism, is a rumour her own testimony contradicts, and no contemporaneous document settles it. Day unrecorded, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The war of June divides nobody in the organisation except her. The question is which side began it, and the group requires that its members agree; she does not, so she goes. Debord's advice, she says, is to stay clandestine, like Jorn, and she takes it: she keeps showing work with them for about three more years. No resignation letter from 1967 has ever surfaced. She will spend decades refusing the word Zionist, and the rumour that she was expelled for it outlives every document that might have settled the matter.
stops.quote: The arguments over this war were long and everyone was in agreement apart from me.
suggested_refs: The Situationist International chronology for 1967, recording her resignation from the French section
sources: Frieze, 'The Game', interview with Michèle Bernstein (2013), via text proxy

stops.name: Paris, the Sorbonne: the festival
stops.date_confidence: The occupation of the Sorbonne, 14 May 1968, is attested and the coordinate is inherited byte-identically from guy_debord.journey.json. Bernstein's own presence inside the occupied building is not documented: the dossier's details, bicycling for cigarettes and helping make a banner, were confirmed by nothing reached. What is attested is her later prose on May 1968, the 2018 preface to Walter Lewino's L'Imagination au pouvoir, from which the quotation is taken.
stops.campa: The Sorbonne is occupied, and the slogans going up on its walls are the ones the organisation she left last year has been printing for a decade to an audience of five or six. She is thirty-six and a member of nothing, having resigned before any of this began. Whether she went inside the building is documented nowhere. Fifty years on she writes the preface to a book of photographs of that month, and what she puts down first is not what the occupation achieved but what it felt like to be in it.
stops.quote: Everyone who was there will tell you that it was, first and foremost, a festival.
stops.quote_source: Michèle Bernstein, 'Hot Water on All Floors', preface to Walter Lewino, L'Imagination au pouvoir (Allia, 2018), NOT BORED! translation
suggested_refs: Walter Lewino and Jo Schnapp, L'Imagination au pouvoir (1968; Éditions Allia, 2018), with her preface
sources: notbored.org, 'Hot Water on All Floors' PDF

stops.name: Paris: the divorce
stops.date_confidence: 5 January 1972 attested (en.wikipedia: the marriage 'was officially ended January 5, 1972'); the Yale finding aid gives the year only, contrary to the research pool's citation. Her stated reason is verbatim from the Frieze interview 'The Game' (2013), reached through a text proxy. No source names the tribunal; the coordinate is the Paris pin guy_debord.journey.json carries for this marriage, inherited unchanged.
stops.campa: The marriage has been over for years and ends on paper on the fifth of January. The reason is a flat she is buying and the liabilities of a journal whose organisation she left five years ago. No tribunal is named in any record reached, and no lawyer either. She is thirty-nine. Later that same year Debord marries Alice Becker-Ho. The novels that helped pay for the group through the 1960s were hers, and the flat she is buying is bought on what she earns.
stops.quote: I was buying my flat and no longer wanted to be responsible, as Guy's wife, for any financial costs or fines that the IS journal could have.
suggested_refs: The 1954-1972 marriage of Michèle Bernstein and Guy Debord

stops.name: Canterbury: the second marriage
stops.date_confidence: End of 1973 attested from Bernstein's own words in the Frieze interview, which settles the disagreement with secondary notices giving 1974; day and month unrecorded, and December is an ordering device. Rumney's teaching at the Canterbury College of Art and his 1958 marriage to Pegeen Vail Guggenheim, who died 1 March 1967, are attested (en.wikipedia), which also disagrees with fr.wikipedia on whether his expulsion came seven or nine months after the founding, both landing in 1958. Bernstein's own residence in Canterbury is uncorroborated: the Frieze interview names only Salisbury.
stops.campa: She marries Ralph Rumney, who was expelled from the Situationist International within a year of helping found it beside her, and who is the widower of Peggy Guggenheim's daughter Pegeen. He teaches at the art college in Canterbury, and has done for years. Debord's response is exclusion, pronounced over a woman who had resigned from the organisation six years earlier. Her own account of all this is one sentence, written forty years afterward. She is not recorded as answering him at the time, by her or by anybody else.
stops.quote: At the end of '73, Ralph and I married. Debord went into a rage, and this time excluded me for good.
suggested_refs: Ralph Rumney, Le Consul (1999), his account of the Situationist years

stops.name: Salisbury: the house and the bicycle
stops.date_confidence: 1982 attested for the move to Salisbury, given in the same sentence as the start at Libération (fr.wikipedia). Month and day unrecorded, defaulted to 01-01. The 'Old Parsonage' address given in the dossier was not corroborated by the page fetched and is not stated. Coordinate marks the historic cathedral close, not a confirmed address. Between the 1973 marriage and this year no English town is recorded for her anywhere.
stops.campa: She settles at Salisbury, a cathedral city of fifty thousand people in the south of England, and is seen riding a bicycle around its streets. She is fifty, and by her own account Salisbury is where she goes after leaving Rumney. Between the marriage at the end of 1973 and this address there are nine years for which no English town is recorded in anything reached. The house named in the secondary accounts is corroborated by nothing, and is not named here. The same year, she starts reviewing books in Paris.
suggested_refs: Salisbury Cathedral Close, the quarter the sources place her in

stops.name: Paris, Libération: fourteen years of reviewing
stops.date_confidence: 1982 to 1996 attested from Bernstein's own words in the Frieze interview, quoted here, and from fr.wikipedia for the 1982 start; month unrecorded, and June is an ordering device. Her account corrects the dossier, which had Serge July ignorant of her past until Lebovici's 1984 murder: she says he did not know for two years, and that the murder prompted him to ask her to write about Debord. The coordinate is Libération's rue Béranger office, a later address, and does not hold for the whole tenure.
stops.campa: Approached around her fiftieth birthday, she joins the book pages of Libération and starts reviewing. She champions Marie NDiaye, Lydie Salvayre and Hervé Guibert while they are still young enough to need it. Serge July, who runs the paper, does not learn for two years that his literary critic is Guy Debord's first wife. It takes the murder of Gérard Lebovici in 1984 to put the name back in the news, and then July asks her to write about him, which she does.
stops.quote: I worked there for 14 years, until 1996 when I was 64, the longest job I ever had, and I liked it.
suggested_refs: The book pages of Libération, 1982-1996

stops.name: Paris: the review of Le Protocole compassionnel
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The date and the subject come from the dossier's bibliography of her Libération criticism; the article itself was never located or read in any pass, and nothing here goes beyond what that bibliography states. Coordinate is the Libération office pin, with the same caveat as the previous stop.
stops.campa: On the twenty-first of February she reviews Hervé Guibert's Le Protocole compassionnel, the second of the books he wrote while dying of AIDS, and takes his side against the objections it is going to draw. She is fifty-eight and has been on the book pages for nine years, long enough that her byline carries weight in Paris. The article itself has not been recovered; no copy of it was located anywhere, and a single line in a bibliography of her criticism is the only trace left of it.
suggested_refs: Hervé Guibert, Le Protocole compassionnel (Gallimard, 1991)
sources: Dossier bibliography of Bernstein's Libération criticism (article not located)

stops.name: Paris: leaving the paper at sixty-four
stops.date_confidence: 1996 attested from her own words in the Frieze interview: fourteen years, ending in 1996 at sixty-four, which checks against a 1932 birth. Month and day unrecorded, defaulted to 01-01. Coordinate is the Libération office pin.
stops.campa: She stops at sixty-four, fourteen years after starting, and calls it the longest job she ever had. Before it there was the publishing house at tuppence ha'penny, a cabaret for a few months, copy for a racing paper, two novels and a journal that sold five or six copies an issue. The book pages of a daily paper turn out to be the steadiest employment in a life spent among people who wrote on walls that nobody should ever work. She does not take another job after it.
suggested_refs: Guy Debord's rue de Seine graffito, NE TRAVAILLEZ JAMAIS (1953)

segments.name: The Hamlet, and What Came Back

stops.name: Normandy: the house in the hamlet
stops.date_confidence: About twenty years of residence, running to the early 2020s, is attested from the Kinsella profile (partisanhotel.co.uk), which also carries her judgement on the windows; the start year is inferred from that span and is not itself documented. The village is withheld in every source reached, and the coordinate is a nominal placeholder inside Normandy, not the hamlet. The dossier's basket of provisions, magnifying glass, and reading distortions were not found on the page fetched and are not stated.
stops.campa: She moves to a house in a hamlet outside a small village in Normandy and stays about twenty years. She dislikes the windows, which are large and let in more of the country than she wants, and calls them depressing. The village is named by nobody who writes about her, and she does not name it either. Of the inside of the house almost nothing is recorded until a telephone call two decades on, made by a translator who cannot travel. She is still in the house when it comes, approaching ninety, in a place she chose and does not much like.
suggested_refs: Clodagh Kinsella's profile of Bernstein in Normandy, partisanhotel.co.uk

stops.name: Normandy: the preface in the guise of an autobiography
stops.date_confidence: The preface is dated 2013 and was published with the Book Works edition of The Night; text read at theanarchistlibrary.org. Month and day unrecorded, defaulted to 01-01. Coordinate is her Normandy pin: the preface was written where she was living, and no place of composition is stated in the source.
stops.campa: An English translation of the second novel is coming out, fifty-two years after the French, and at eighty-one she writes a preface for it. It explains the counterfeit: the skint year of 1957, the humdrum publishing house, the decision to fabricate a popular novel and sell it. Book Works publishes it in London with Clodagh Kinsella's translation. It explains the drift too, and refuses the word hobby for that. The last paragraph names what the book is about.
stops.quote: And if La Nuit is a love story, it's not for him or for her, or for someone else, or for me. It's a love story, a story of lost love. For the streets.
stops.quote_source: Michèle Bernstein, 'Preface in the Guise of an Autobiography, or Vice Versa' (2013)
suggested_refs: Michèle Bernstein, The Night, trans. Clodagh Kinsella (Book Works, 2013)
sources: Michèle Bernstein, 'Preface in the Guise of an Autobiography, or Vice Versa' (2013), theanarchistlibrary.org

stops.name: Normandy: the letter to Raoul Vaneigem
stops.date_confidence: 3 August 2014 attested; text from the NOT BORED! translation, extracted directly from the notbored.org PDF and published in Rien n'est fini, tout commence (Allia, 2014). Coordinate is her Normandy pin; no place of writing is given. The research pool framed a second quotation from this letter as advice she gave Nicole; the letter says the opposite, that she was far away and never gave it, and that framing is not used here.
stops.campa: She writes to Raoul Vaneigem on the third of August about people forty and fifty years gone: Henri Lefebvre, the sociologist, and a woman called Cheype. The subject is who was fond of whom in those years, and who was not, and she names them without softening any of it. The letter is printed the same year by Allia, in a collection whose title announces that nothing is finished and everything is beginning. She is eighty-two. Debord has been dead twenty years.
stops.quote: Of all of Guy's little lovers, Cheype is the only one who had antipathy for me (I even remained friends with several of them).
stops.quote_source: Michèle Bernstein, letter to Raoul Vaneigem, 3 August 2014, in Rien n'est fini, tout commence (Allia, 2014), NOT BORED! translation
suggested_refs: Michèle Bernstein, Rien n'est fini, tout commence (Éditions Allia, 2014)

stops.name: Paris: the papers sold
stops.date_confidence: 2019 attested from the Yale finding aid's acquisition note, recording the purchase from Bernstein and the bookseller Didier Lecointre-Dominique Drouet on the Edwin J. Beinecke Book Fund; the collection is GEN MSS 1556, seven boxes. The 2022 opening of the poems is attested from postwarcultureatbeinecke.org. Month and day unrecorded, defaulted to 01-01. The stop sits at her own Paris pin: the selling is hers, and the New Haven end of it is the library's.
stops.campa: She sells the boxes: the letters from Debord, the twenty-two poems, the notebook explaining them, the photographs from Moineau's, the corrected proofs of every issue of the journal. The buyer is Yale, through a Paris bookseller, and the papers cross the Atlantic to a reading room in Connecticut. Sixty-five years of it, seven boxes, catalogued as GEN MSS 1556. Three years later the twenty-two poems are opened to readers for the first time. She is eighty-seven.
suggested_refs: The Michèle Bernstein Papers, GEN MSS 1556, purchased by the Beinecke Library in 2019
sources: Yale Beinecke, Guide to the Michèle Bernstein Papers, Immediate Source of Acquisition

stops.name: Normandy: the telephone in the viral winter
stops.date_confidence: Winter 2020 to 2021 attested from the Kinsella profile (partisanhotel.co.uk), describing the telephone contact during 'the viral winter of 2020' and the Normandy visit that did not happen. Month is an ordering device inside that winter, day defaulted to 01. The quotation is rendered in capitals in the source. Coordinate is her Normandy pin.
stops.campa: Her English translator telephones during the closed winter of 2020, meaning to come to Normandy and unable to. They talk on the line instead. Bernstein is eighty-eight and opens with a sentence the translator will use twice as a title, once for a profile and once for a short film. The film is called On the Passage of Michèle Bernstein Through Time. Debord had called his, in 1959, On the Passage of a Few Persons Through a Rather Brief Unity of Time.
stops.quote_source: Michèle Bernstein to Clodagh Kinsella, winter 2020, quoted at partisanhotel.co.uk
suggested_refs: Clodagh Kinsella, On the Passage of Michèle Bernstein Through Time (film, 2021)

stops.name: Paris, Montparnasse: the meeting by the cemetery
stops.date_confidence: The meeting is attested from the Kinsella profile, which places it near the Jewish section of Montparnasse Cemetery and by a plaque marking a former Simone de Beauvoir residence; no exact date is given, and 2021 is taken from the profile's year. Month and day defaulted to 01-01. Coordinate is the cemetery's western edge.
stops.campa: They meet in the end in Paris, near the Jewish section of the Montparnasse cemetery, by a wall carrying a plaque for a flat Simone de Beauvoir once lived in, a hundred metres from the graves. She is eighty-nine, and has outlived nearly everyone who was in the room at Cosio d'Arroscia. Asked about her place in a history other people have spent fifty years writing, she answers in one sentence and does not soften it. The Normandy visit never happened; this is the meeting instead.
stops.quote: I am an orange that's already been sucked.
stops.quote_source: Michèle Bernstein to Clodagh Kinsella, quoted at partisanhotel.co.uk
suggested_refs: The Jewish section of the Montparnasse cemetery, Paris 14e

stops.name: Normandy: the postface
stops.date_confidence: The second English edition and its new postface are attested from the Book Works page for The Night; 2021 is that edition's year and the month is an ordering device. The research pool described the addition as prefatory and postface material, which overstates it: the publisher names a postface only. Everyone Agrees' After the Night (Book Works, 2013) is other people's work in another city and is cited here rather than staged. Coordinate is her Normandy pin.
stops.campa: A second English edition of the second novel comes out, and at eighty-nine she adds a postface. The confession in it is about the drift: that a reader might take the book for the record of a life spent walking Paris, and that she does not want that credited to her. Sixty years after the novel she is still refusing to be read straight. In the same catalogue sits a London collective's rewrite of the book, made eight years earlier and set in East London.
stops.quote: I am a fraud. Anyone who buys The Night (thank you) and so much as skims it might think that I used to spend my time walking the streets of Paris...
stops.quote_source: Michèle Bernstein, postface to the second edition of The Night (Book Works, 2021)
suggested_refs: Everyone Agrees, After the Night (Book Works, 2013), a détournement of La Nuit set in London

stops.name: Paris, 76 rue de Turenne: sitting for the painter
stops.date_confidence: The exhibition ran 23 November 2024 to 18 January 2025 at Perrotin, 76 rue de Turenne, and the two portraits, the roughly three-hour single-session sittings, and the quoted description are attested from the press release PDF, read directly. The sittings themselves are undated and the studio address is undocumented, so the coordinate is the gallery, corrected: the research pool carried two different pins for the same address. The dossier's titles for the two portraits belong to other canvases and are not used. This is the most recent evidence found anywhere that Bernstein was alive; no death record or obituary has been located, and none is claimed here.
stops.campa: A painter who works next door to her, and is her friend, asks her to sit. She does, twice, from life, with no photographs taken, about three hours each time and usually finished in a single session. The canvases go up in a gallery on the rue de Turenne on the twenty-third of November. The press text gives the sitter's age, ninety-two, and reads the slowness of the procedure as a refusal of the society of the spectacle. The show runs until the eighteenth of January.
stops.quote: the cofounder of one of the last avant-garde movements, the Situationist International
stops.quote_source: Perrotin, press release for Jean-Philippe Delhomme, 'Model Resting' (2024), text by Valérie Da Costa
suggested_refs: Jean-Philippe Delhomme, 'Model Resting', Perrotin Paris, 23 November 2024 to 18 January 2025
sources: static.perrotin.com, press release for 'Model Resting', text by Valérie Da Costa
